name: Overbite / deep bite theory

card.summary: The community idea that a deep vertical overbite shortens the lower face and recesses the chin, so correcting it with orthodontics improves lower-third proportions.
card.note: Dental overbite and a skeletal Class II jaw are different problems; an orthodontist assesses which applies.

quick.overview:
An overbite is the vertical overlap of the upper front teeth over the lower ones; a normal overbite is about 30 to 50% of the lower incisor height, and a deep bite is more overlap than that [1][2]. In looksmaxxing forums, deep bite theory holds that a deep bite shortens the lower third of the face and makes the chin look recessed.
The appearance payoff is claimed to come from correcting the bite with braces, aligners or surgery, so the lower face looks longer and the chin and jawline better balanced. Orthodontic trials do show deep bite can be reduced, though measured effects are in millimetres.
quick.how: Forum users compare deep bites with overjet and skeletal recession, then ask orthodontists about braces such as Damon braces, clear aligners, bite turbos or surgery. Treatment choices reported in trials include miniscrew intrusion, reverse curve archwires and bite turbos [9][3].
quick.risks: Treatment carries the usual orthodontic risks of long courses and relapse; a trial of clear aligners for molar intrusion measured root resorption [4]. Skeletal discrepancies may need orthognathic surgery per Grokipedia [5]. DIY approaches discussed online are not clinically studied.

lead: An overbite is the vertical overlap of the upper incisors over the lower incisors, measured at the biting edges; Wikipedia gives a normal overbite as roughly 30 to 50% of the lower incisor height and says it is often confused with overjet, the horizontal overlap [1]. A deep bite (also called a Type II malocclusion or deep overbite) is a bite in which the upper front teeth cover the lower ones more than that, and Wikipedia's malocclusion article puts it at about 15 to 20% of the US population [2][11].

In looksmaxxing communities the 'deep bite theory' holds that a deep bite shortens the lower third of the face, lowers ramus and mandible height and makes the chin look recessed, so that correcting the bite with braces, aligners or jaw surgery gives a longer, better-balanced lower face. A looksmax.org thread from a coaching forum states that more than 25% coverage is a deep bite and that worse deep bites mean a shorter lower third [6]. Other posters ask whether Damon braces will fix a deep bite, whether bite correction needs extension fillers, and whether a deep bite can weaken zygomatic projection [7][18][19].

Orthodontic literature describes the bite itself in more detail than the facial claims. A systematic review of 53 studies put deep overbite at about 22% worldwide, with open bite at about 5% [8]. A 2025 systematic review of randomised trials in deep bite correction found that miniscrew-supported intrusion produced a small but significant overbite reduction (mean difference about 0.36 mm) [9]. Wikipedia's malocclusion article notes that decreased vertical facial growth tends to produce a short face, often with a deep bite [11].

chain: Lower face height and bite relationship change
angle.text: Proponents say correcting a deep bite lengthens the lower face and improves the chin profile; orthodontic research confirms bites can be corrected, with effects measured in millimetres.

paras: Overbite is measured as vertical overlap, whereas overjet is the horizontal distance between the upper and lower front teeth. Wikipedia states that the word overbite does not itself name a specific condition and that an absent or excessive overbite would be the malocclusion; it adds that the term is sometimes loosely used for Class II malocclusion or for a retrognathic (set-back) lower jaw, a usage it calls incorrect [1][13].

Grokipedia classes overbite as dental (tooth tilt or position), skeletal (jaw growth or position) or mixed, and links deep bite with Angle Class II, especially division 2 [5]. Angle's classification, based on the relationship of the upper and lower first molars, dates to 1899 and was popularised by Edward Angle, often called the father of modern orthodontics [11]. Class II division 2 is the pattern in which the upper central incisors tip backward and the bite is deep [11].

Wikipedia's malocclusion article lists skeletal, muscular and dental contributors, including jaw size and position, childhood diet and chewing, mouth breathing, habits such as thumb or pacifier sucking, and tooth size or eruption problems [11]. Grokipedia additionally lists polygenic inheritance and syndromes that cause jaw underdevelopment [5]. A 2021 meta-analysis reviewed how mouth breathing in children relates to facial skeletal development and malocclusion [10].

Overbite has long been discussed in anthropology as well as dentistry. Wikipedia reports that the American anthropologist C. Loring Brace proposed that the European overbite is only a few centuries old and followed the adoption of the table knife and fork, and that Steven Moran and Balthasar Bickel suggested in 2019 that labiodental speech sounds may have developed alongside it; the article presents the latter as speculation [1].

In looksmaxxing spaces the concept appears as 'deep bite' and 'overbite' threads on looksmax.org, where posters mix the dental measurement with ideas about jaw recession, lower-third length and chin projection. Titles in this cluster include questions on fixing a deep bite without surgery, DIY orthodontics and the relationship between overbite and a recessed mandible [6][7][18][19][20]. One thread is posted by a coaching-forum author who promotes bite correction as a route to a better jaw aesthetic [6].

A coaching-forum thread posted to looksmax.org says deep bite shortens the lower third and reduces ramus height, sorts bites into mild, normal and severe categories by percentage of coverage, and links severe bites with masseter and TMJ problems and 'short face syndrome' [6]. Another thread's author, who reports 6 teeth showing in a smile and prominent zygomas, asks what to know before starting Damon braces and is told by a reply to ask for extension fillers at the back of the teeth during treatment [19].

A poster who sees a recessed chin and jawline in photos and finds that jutting the jaw forward makes the profile look stronger asks how to fix it; one reply says orthodontics resolved the same look for them, while another says the profile is normal and that upper-jaw recession would show in the nose [20]. Other threads ask whether a deep bite can weaken zygomatic projection and whether anything besides braces can fix a severe deep bite [18][21].

Orthodontic correction of a deep bite works by levelling the bite, which clinicians describe as intruding the upper incisors, extruding the lower incisors, or both; Grokipedia gives a typical fixed-brace course as 18 to 24 months [5]. Mild to moderate cases are described as suited to clear aligners, with efficacy said to fall in deeper bites; children may receive growth-modifying appliances such as the Herbst appliance or headgear, and severe adult skeletal cases may be treated with orthognathic surgery [5]. Wikipedia's malocclusion article lists functional appliances, headgear, camouflage and orthognathic surgery as Class II options and braces or removable appliances, sometimes with surgery, for deep bite [11].

Whether bite correction changes lower-face height or chin position depends on the type of problem. Wikipedia describes skeletal disharmonies between the jaws as able to distort facial shape and often needing orthognathic surgery, which can move the chin forward through genioplasty or the whole lower jaw through bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and typically produces a noticeable change in facial appearance [11][12]. Grokipedia says overbite can bring a convex profile and a shorter lower face that makes the chin look receded, but that a deep bite does not cause recession of the upper midface [5]. Comparisons of before-and-after facial height in deep bite treatment are mostly measured in cephalometric millimetres rather than appearance ratings [9][3].

Mouth breathing in children has been reviewed for effects on facial skeletal development and malocclusion in a 2021 meta-analysis [10]. A 2025 meta-analysis of deep bite treatments found miniscrew-supported intrusion reduced overbite by a small amount [9]. A randomised trial of 48 patients compared a reverse curve of Spee archwire with anterior bite turbos [3].

A Cochrane review of orthodontic treatment for deep bite with retroclined upper front teeth in children (Millett and colleagues, 2018 update) searched trial registries and databases to November 2017 and found no randomised or controlled clinical trials meeting its criteria, so it reports no treatment comparison; the authors cite low prevalence, recruitment difficulty and ethical concerns about randomising children as obstacles [14][15]. Wikipedia's malocclusion article summarises that the evidence for deep bite treatment success is not robust [11].

Studies of open bite, the opposite vertical pattern, include a meta-analysis of six studies with a mean follow-up of 2.5 years that found a mean overbite relapse of about 1.2 mm after molar intrusion with skeletal anchorage [16]. Prevalence reviews report that malocclusion is common: a 2020 meta-analysis of 77 studies put worldwide malocclusion prevalence in children and adolescents at 56% [17].

Orthodontic treatment involves multi-month to multi-year courses and retainers afterwards; Grokipedia says retainers are essential to keep results and reports partial relapse in about 20 to 30% of mandibular advancements [5]. A randomised trial of 40 adults compared clear aligners with fixed appliances plus miniscrews for molar intrusion and measured root resorption of the molars at six months [4].

Orthognathic surgery is described by Wikipedia as carrying risks of bleeding, swelling, infection and temporary facial numbness, with recovery measured in weeks to months and orthodontic phases before and after surgery [12]. Grokipedia reports temporary numbness in many patients, usually resolving within 6 to 12 months, and a soft-diet period of four to six weeks [5]. Wikipedia adds that malocclusion can affect self-esteem when it significantly affects appearance and that tooth wear and gum problems are among the functional concerns [11]. DIY orthodontics, which appears in forum thread titles, has not been clinically studied [20].

A 2018 systematic review pooled 53 studies and put deep overbite at about 22% and open bite at about 5% worldwide [8]. A 2025 review of eight randomised trials of deep bite correction reported a small but significant overbite reduction with miniscrew-supported intrusion [9]. A 2022 randomised trial of 48 patients, mean overbite about 5 to 6 mm, compared a lower reverse curve of Spee nickel-titanium archwire with metal anterior bite turbos [3]. A 2023 randomised trial of 40 adults with anterior open bite compared clear aligners with fixed appliances plus miniscrews for molar intrusion and measured root resorption, intrusion amount and bite force [4]. The Cochrane review of deep bite with retroclined upper incisors in children reports no eligible controlled trials [14][15]. No published study has measured lower-third length or chin projection before and after deep bite correction as the forum theory describes it.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known cases of jaw surgery, the lineage of later orthognathic procedures [12]
The English term malocclusion first appears, later popularised by Edward Angle [11]
Edward Angle publishes his classification of malocclusion by molar relationship [11]
Osteotomies of the mandible and maxilla first used, with Hugo Obwegeser later developing the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy [12]
First Cochrane review of orthodontic treatment for deep bite with retroclined upper incisors in children, later updated in 2017 and 2018 [14][15]
Systematic review of 53 studies puts worldwide deep overbite prevalence at about 22% [8]
Moran and Bickel propose in The Conversation that overbite may have shaped speech sounds, cited as speculation [1]
Randomised trial compares reverse curve archwires with anterior bite turbos for deep overbite [3]
Randomised trial measures root resorption during molar intrusion with clear aligners [4]
Systematic review of eight randomised trials evaluates methods of correcting deep bite [9]

lore.intro: Deep bite appears on looksmax.org as both a dental problem and a suspected cause of a recessed chin and short lower third, with coaching-forum authors and individual posters discussing braces, aligners, surgery and DIY approaches [6][7][18][19][20].

claims.claim: A deep bite shortens the lower third and recesses the chin
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread says severe deep bites decrease ramus and mandible height and cause short-face traits [6].
claims.experts: Wikipedia links reduced vertical facial growth with a short profile and deep bite [11]; Grokipedia says overbite can give a shorter lower face that makes the chin look receded [5]. Whether bite correction lengthens the lower face has not been measured.

claims.claim: Anything past 25% coverage is a deep bite
claims.believers: A coaching-forum thread uses 25% as the cutoff and sorts bites into mild and severe categories [6].
claims.experts: Wikipedia gives a normal overbite as roughly 30 to 50% of lower incisor height, a different range from the forum cutoff [1].

claims.claim: A deep bite weakens zygomatic projection
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether a deep bite can reduce lateral zygomatic projection [18].
claims.experts: Grokipedia states that deep bite does not cause upper midface recession [5]; no published study has tested a link with the zygomatic bone.

claims.claim: Braces can fix a deep bite and improve the profile
claims.believers: Posters report that braces resolved a recessed-looking chin and jawline, and ask about Damon braces for deep bites [19][20].
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis found small overbite reductions with miniscrew intrusion, and trials compare archwires with bite turbos [9][3]; the Cochrane review for children with retroclined upper incisors found no eligible trials [14][15].

claims.claim: Overbite and a recessed lower jaw are the same thing
claims.believers: Threads use 'overbite' for a set-back chin and ask how to fix it [20].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says overbite is a vertical tooth overlap and that using the word for Class II or retrognathia is loose usage; Class II involves the molar relationship [1][13][11].

claims.claim: A deep bite can be corrected without surgery
claims.believers: Threads discuss braces, aligners, extension fillers and DIY orthodontics as non-surgical routes [19][20].
claims.experts: Orthodontic treatment of dental deep bite is described in trials and reviews; Grokipedia says severe adult skeletal cases may need orthognathic surgery [9][5].
